t.6.77.1: Seeing those two, the man and the Rākṣasa, locked in combat and fighting on, that heroic brother of Rāvaṇa stood at the forefront of the battle.
t.6.77.2: Then, standing firm, he stretched his mighty bow and loosed great sharp-pointed arrows upon the rākṣasas.
t.6.77.3: Those arrows, resembling fire, well aimed and falling upon them, tore the Rākṣasas apart, as thunderbolts split great mountains.
t.6.77.4: Those followers of Vibhīṣaṇa too, the foremost of rākṣasas, cut down the heroic rākṣasas in battle with spears, swords and paṭṭisas.
t.6.77.5: Then Vibhīṣaṇa, surrounded by those rākṣasas, shone like a great elephant in the midst of exultant young elephant calves.
t.6.77.7: This one alone stands as if he were the last refuge of the lord of the Rākṣasas; this is all that remains of his army. Why do you stand idle, O lords of the monkeys?
t.6.77.8: When this wicked rākṣasa has been slain at the forefront of battle, then, apart from Rāvaṇa, the rest of his army is as good as destroyed.
t.6.77.6: Then the best of the rākṣasas, who knew the right moment, urged on the monkeys, who delighted in battle with the rākṣasas, and spoke these words at that fitting time.
t.6.77.9: The heroic Prahasta has been slain, and the mighty Nikumbha, and Kumbhakarṇa, and Kumbha, and the night-roaming Dhūmrākṣa as well.
t.6.77.10: Akampana and Supārśva, and the rākṣasa Cakramālī, Kampana, and the mighty Devāntaka and Narāntaka,
t.6.77.11: Having slain these many exceedingly mighty, foremost rākṣasas, as one who has crossed the ocean with his own arms, let the little cow's hoofprint now be leapt over.
t.6.77.12: O monkeys, this much alone remains here for you to conquer; all the rākṣasas, proud of their strength, have been slain, once they came together in battle.
t.6.77.13: It is improper for me, who stand as a father to him, to bring about the death of a son; yet, casting aside pity for Rāma's sake, I would slay my brother's son.
t.6.77.14: Though I wish to kill him, tears rise and my eyes are blinded. Therefore this mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa will bring that to an end, and let the monkeys band together to kill his attendants who stand near him.
t.6.77.16: Then those tigers among monkeys, roaring again and again, let forth cries of many kinds, like peacocks on seeing the rain clouds.
t.6.77.15: Thus urged by that most illustrious rākṣasa, the lords of the monkeys rejoiced and lashed their tails.
t.6.77.17: Jāmbavān too, surrounded by all those troops of his own, struck the rākṣasas with stones, with his claws and with his teeth.
t.6.77.18: Casting aside their fear, those mighty rākṣasas, bearing weapons of many kinds, surrounded the lord of the ṛkṣas as he was striking them down.
t.6.77.19: With arrows, sharp axes, paṭṭisas, staves and lances they struck Jāmbavant in battle as he was slaying the rākṣasa army.
t.6.77.20: That tumultuous clash arose between the monkeys and the Rākṣasas, terrible and loud-roaring, like that of the enraged gods and Asuras.
t.6.77.21: Hanūmān too, greatly enraged, uprooted a sāla tree from the mountain and, falling upon the rākṣasas, made a slaughter of them by the thousands.
t.6.77.22: Having given his paternal uncle a tumultuous fight in battle, Indrajit rushed once again at Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes.
t.6.77.23: Then those two heroes, Lakṣmaṇa and the Rākṣasa, fiercely engaged in battle, showering floods of arrows, struck each other.
t.6.77.24: Again and again the two mighty and powerful warriors vanished beneath nets of arrows, just as the moon and the sun are hidden by clouds at the end of the hot season.
t.6.77.25: Neither the taking up nor the fitting of arrows, nor the grasping of the bow, nor the release of the shafts, nor the drawing back, nor the separation could be perceived.
t.6.77.26: Such was the swiftness of their hands that, as the two fought there, neither the fitting of arrows in their grip nor their aiming at the target could be seen.
t.6.77.27: As the sky was covered on all sides by networks of arrows loosed with the force of the bows, no forms could be seen. Everything was veiled in darkness, and it became vast and even more terrible.
t.6.77.28: At that time the wind did not blow, nor did fire blaze, and the great sages murmured, "May there be well-being for the worlds!" The Gandharvas, together with the Cāraṇas, arrived and flew together there.
t.6.77.29: Then Saumitri, with four arrows, pierced the four black horses, adorned with gold, of that lion among rākṣasas.
t.6.77.31: Seeing his charioteer slain in battle, the son of Rāvaṇa gave up his eagerness for combat and became despondent.
t.6.77.30: Then, with another broad-headed arrow, the glorious Rāghava, through his swiftness of hand, struck the head of the charioteer from his body as he was about to wheel about.
t.6.77.33: Then Pramāthī, Śarabha, Rabhasa and Gandhamādana, those four lords of the monkeys, unable to endure it, rushed forward with great speed.
t.6.77.32: Seeing the rākṣasa with his face downcast, the leaders of the monkey troops, filled with the greatest delight, then honored Lakṣmaṇa.
t.6.77.34: And those monkeys, exceedingly mighty and of fearsome valour, swiftly leapt up and fell upon his four foremost horses.
t.6.77.35: As those horses were mounted by the vānaras, who were like mountains, blood plainly streamed forth from their mouths.
t.6.77.36: Having slain his horses and smashed his great chariot, they leapt up again with speed and stood at Lakṣmaṇa's side.
t.6.77.37: Leaping down from his chariot, whose horses were slain and whose charioteer was crushed, Rāvaṇi rushed at Saumitri with a shower of arrows.
t.6.77.38: Then Lakṣmaṇa, the equal of great Indra, with sharp and excellent arrows and with volleys of shafts, forcefully held back his foe, who was now on foot and who had first been loosing sharp and excellent arrows.
